nodes.label: Q20: Securing microservices, JWT and OAuth
JWT
nodes.rationale: Signed, not encrypted — anyone holding it reads every claim, so it is not a place to cache a profile. Validation is a signature check against an in-memory key, which is what makes it scale and also what makes it impossible to revoke; hence 30-minute lifetimes paired with a revocable refresh token.

nodes.label: OAuth 2.0 vs OpenID Connect
nodes.rationale: OAuth answers 'may this application act on the user's behalf'; OIDC adds 'and here is who the user is' as an ID token. Authorization code + PKCE is the correct default; ROPC (used here for curl convenience) is discouraged in OAuth 2.1 because the app handles the real password, ruling out MFA, federation and consent.

nodes.label: Token relay between services
nodes.rationale: Forwarding the user's token means downstream services see the real caller and their real roles. Client credentials would be right for background work but wrong here — it gives every request the gateway's permissions and makes downstream logs say 'gateway did this'. The first version called four services anonymously and got four 401s.

nodes.label: Every service validates the JWT again
nodes.rationale: The gateway is not the only way in — another service, a debugging shell or an attacker past the edge can call directly. 'Inside the cluster' is not a trust boundary, and re-validation costs microseconds.

nodes.label: HS256 shared symmetric key — a known limitation
nodes.rationale: Every service needs the signing key just to validate, so any one of them could mint tokens for all the others, and rotating the key means redeploying everything. Production uses RS256/ES256 with a JWKS endpoint so rotation is a non-event.

nodes.label: Secure by default (fallback authorization policy)
nodes.rationale: A RequireAuthenticatedUser fallback closes any endpoint that forgets to declare a policy; forgetting [Authorize] is far more common than forgetting AllowAnonymous, and only one of those is a breach. Related: PBKDF2 with per-user salt and fixed-time comparison, refresh-token rotation as a theft signal, and roles as policies so adding a role changes one definition.

nodes.label: 401 vs 403
nodes.rationale: 401 means 'I do not know who you are'; 403 means 'I know and you may not'. Returning 401 for an authorisation failure tells an authenticated user to log in again, which in a browser is an infinite loop.
